text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Speculation in Bonn that Helmut Kohl may put off deciding whether to stand again for chancellorship in 1998 general election until just before the summer holidays.
- United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan due to visit Germany from April 16 to 18.
- Germany strongly rejects criticism by Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan over the deaths of three Turks in a fatal fire in the country.
- German Trade Union Congress (DGB) wants to hold up third stage of health reforms which would lead to a rise in health insurance contributions.
HANDELSBLATT
- German unions IG Chemie and DAG criticise strategy of opposition Social Democrat (SDP) leader Oskar Lafontaine over tax refrom. Unions demand the SDP comes up with complete tax plans of their own.
- German export business continues to climb, with 64.4 billion marks worth of goods exported in January.
- German chemicals giant BASF AG says it expects to post stronger 1997 earnings and an increase in sales, benefiting from the global economic recovery.

- Labour Minister Norbert Bluem and head of the Federal Association of German Industry (BDI) Hans-Olaf Henkel exhange harsh words over business strategy of German companies after attempted hostile takeover in steel industry.
- Labour Ministry says tariff wages and salaries climbed by an average of 1.8 percent in 1996, less than in 1995.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Tariff wages and salaries climb less in 1996 than 1995.
- Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok tells German newspaper European monetary union (EMU), set to begin in 1999, can only be launched on time if both Germany and France participate.
- Labour Minister Bluem and the BDI's Henkel argue over behaviour of German companies.
- Bavarian Finance Minister Otto Wiesheu says Landesanstalt fuer Aufbaufinazierung (LfA) can continue to offer credit lines of over 50 million marks to businesses.
- Dispute intensifies between Germany and Turkey over recent arson attacks.
DIE WELT
- Bonn rejects criticism by Turkish Prime Minister Erkaban over recent arson attacks.
- Government plans to cut welfare benefits widely rejected. SPD says will energetically resist plans.
- BASF AG reports record turnover of 46.6 billion marks in 1996, 5.5 percent more than the year before.
